blocks.c: I did not press it that night either.
What I did was go up to the eleventh floor, to the facilities office, where there is a grey steel cabinet nobody opens, and I opened it.
Inside: forty years of maintenance logs.
Bound books, one per year, in order, going back to 1974. The oldest ones are green. Sometime in the eighties they go to blue. In 2011 somebody switched to the black ones we use now.
I took down the current year. I turned to March. I found my missing entry.
Not in my handwriting. In careful block capitals, in the margin, running vertically up the page, the way you write when you have run out of room and refuse to start a new line:
ENTRY REMOVED FROM THE WORKING LOG BY ARRANGEMENT. RECORDED HERE INSTEAD. THE ARRANGEMENT REQUIRES A RECORD. IT DOES NOT REQUIRE THE RECORD TO BE CONVENIENT.
RULE ONE: WRITE EVERYTHING DOWN. IT CANNOT TAKE WHAT IS WRITTEN DOWN. — W.A.
I stood in that room for a long time with a book in my hands.
Then I did the only sensible thing available, which was to go back four years, and then eight, and then fifteen, looking for the same handwriting.
I found it in every single volume.

Different pens. Same block capitals. Same initials. 2019, 2014, 2008, 2001, 1996. Marginal notes in a building's maintenance log, going back at least thirty years, written by a person who had apparently never aged out of the job.
The oldest one I found that night was in the 1994 book, and it was four words long, and it was not addressed to the building.
IF YOU FOUND THE KEY, DON'T.
